newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: World Gold Council to promote bullion investment.
newsitem.headline: World Gold Council to promote bullion investment.

text.p: The World Gold Council (WGC) will promote gold as an investment asset to institutional investors, WGC officials said at the organisation's annual meeting on Saturday.
It also aims to provide "quality information" on gold's attractions as a reserve asset to central banks.

Richard Scott-Ram, economic advisor to the WGC, said a survey last year of 25 U.S. investment funds showed that over half were interested in investing in gold within a year of the survey and several respondents said they saw gold as a useful long-term insurance asset.
The WGC intends to repeat the exercise this year and approach investors outside of the United States, he said.
The WGC is a gold promotional body sponsored by several of the world's leading gold mining houses.
The U.S. institutuional investment market was valued at $10 trillion of which almost half was controlled by pension funds, Scott-Ram said.
"If only one percent of this was invested in gold this would amount to a meaningful amount of gold offtake," he told delegates.
The survey found that U.S. portfolio managers' awareness of gold was low compared with other assets and several believed it was only worth holding in times of inflation.
But Scott-Ram said gold could be an "appropriate" investment against a likely correction in highly-valued U.S. stock markets.

He said that portfolio diversification into "alternative" assets like real estate was becoming more widely accepted. About $32 billion was invested in alternative investments last year, four times as much as in 1991.
He said the factors governing gold price movements were different from these affecting equity prices leading to a 37 percent chance that gold prices would decline if equity prices increased.
Gold was much more liquid than other alternative assets like real estate or timber land, he said.
Robert Pringle, head of the WGC's Public Policy Centre, told delegates the WGC should provide quality information to central bankers on the role of gold as a reserve asset.
He said recent events like the German and Swiss plans to revalue their gold reserves had been "misinterpreted" as negative by the market.
These banks were "modernising" their reserve asset management like many other countries had done, he said.
"Even if central banks sold gold there is no need to be defensive. It is there to be sold if needed," he said.
Gold would become a more significant reserve asset if monetary union in Europe went ahead as the number of currencies available to bankers to hold in reserve would be diminished, he said.
The public response to proposals to sell gold, including gold from the International Monetary Fund's reserves, had been "furious" and "astonished" proponents of the schemes.
"Politicians have to justify to the public their plans to sell gold," Pringle said, adding that selling gold was much more visible than using foreign exchange reserves to prop up an ailing currency.
The WGC had to provide central banks with acurate analysis of what was happening in the world and how this affected their reserves and it should promote gold as a reserve asset, he said.

It should make clear to the market that central banks buy gold as well as sell it and explain to central bankers that the gold industry and gold consumption worldwide were expanding. --Brian Spoors, Prague Newsroom , 420-2-2423-0003
